> **Audit Rights.** [Party B] shall maintain complete and accurate books and records relating to its performance under this Agreement, including all amounts payable hereunder, in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles consistently applied, and shall retain such records for a period of at least three (3) years following the end of the calendar year to which they relate. [Party A], or an independent certified public accountant designated by [Party A], shall have the right, upon not less than thirty (30) days' prior written notice and during normal business hours, no more than once per calendar year, to inspect and audit such books and records for the purpose of verifying [Party B]'s compliance with the terms of this Agreement and the accuracy of payments and reports made hereunder. If any such audit reveals an underpayment in excess of five percent (5%) for the audited period, [Party B] shall promptly pay the shortfall together with the reasonable cost of the audit.

**Reconstruction**

The three questions map cleanly onto a CUAD-style anti-assignment clause that (1) treats assignment of rights and delegation of duties separately, (2) conditions transfer of obligations on the counterparty's consent, and (3) carves out a collateral assignment to a lender with enforcement rights on default. My best estimate of the source text:

> Neither party may assign this Agreement or any of its rights hereunder, nor delegate any of its obligations hereunder, without the prior written consent of the other party, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Notwithstanding the foregoing, [Party A] may, without such consent, assign its rights to receive payments under this Agreement as collateral security to any bank or other lender, and upon an event of default under the related financing documents such lender may exercise all of [Party A]'s rights hereunder, provided that [Party A] remains liable for all of its obligations under this Agreement. Any purported assignment or delegation in violation of this Section shall be null and void.

**How each question anchors the clause**

- **Assignment vs delegation (Q1)** indicates the clause names both "assign its rights" and "delegate its obligations" as distinct acts, rather than a bare "assign this Agreement" formulation.
- **Consent for transfer of obligations (Q2)** indicates consent is the gating condition and is likely asymmetric: rights may be assignable more freely, obligations only with consent. The "typically required" phrasing hints at a "not unreasonably withheld" qualifier.
- **Creditor rights on default of a secured obligation (Q3)** is the strongest signal. It only arises from a security-interest carve-out: the assigning party pledges its contract rights (usually receivables) to a lender, and the lender may step in and enforce on default.

**What cannot be recovered**

Party names, dollar amounts, dates, section numbers and the lender's identity are not recoverable. All three questions were fully generalized, so they carry no entity-specific residue. The clause type, structure and the collateral carve-out are recoverable with high confidence. The exact qualifiers ("unreasonably withheld", "null and void", continued liability of the assignor) are medium-confidence boilerplate inferred from the clause family, not from the questions.
